nameStory: The Red-winged Longhorn Beetle gets its name from the striking reddish-orange coloration on its wing covers (called elytra) and its impressively long antennae that can be longer than its body. The 'longhorn' name comes from these extended antennae that look like tiny horns protruding from the beetle's head, giving it an almost alien appearance.
description: The Red-winged Longhorn Beetle is a medium-sized beetle with a sleek, elongated body and dramatically long antennae. These beautiful insects are easily recognized by their reddish-orange wing covers and dark head and thorax. Adults typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, not counting their impressive antennae which can extend well beyond their body length. They belong to the longhorn beetle family, one of the largest beetle families in the world.

idTips.label: Wing Cover Color
idTips.description: Bright reddish-orange to rusty red wing covers (elytra) that have a smooth, almost polished appearance when touched gently

idTips.label: Antennae Length
idTips.description: Exceptionally long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond the body length and feel delicate if carefully examined

idTips.label: Head and Thorax
idTips.description: Dark blackish head and thorax that contrasts sharply with the bright wing covers, giving a two-toned appearance

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, elongated beetle with a narrow waist and cylindrical form that feels firm but lightweight when handled

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized beetle roughly the length of your thumbnail, excluding the long antennae

habitat: Look for Red-winged Longhorn Beetles in areas where spirea shrubs grow, including woodland edges, meadows, and gardens throughout New England. They're particularly common in mixed hardwood forests and can often be found on flowers during the day, especially on spirea, elderberry, and other white-flowered shrubs. You might spot them in both lowland and montane areas up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring but are not yet at peak activity. Look for early individuals on newly blooming spirea flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen feeding on flower nectar, particularly spirea blooms. This is the best time for identification and observation.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down significantly. Any remaining individuals become increasingly rare as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active. The species overwinters as larvae developing inside dead or dying wood.

funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Red-winged Longhorn Beetle larvae are wood-boring powerhouses that spend up to two years tunneling through dead hardwood, creating intricate galleries that can weaken entire branches - yet the adults are gentle flower visitors that couldn't bite you if they tried!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other red longhorn beetles, but the Red-winged Longhorn's bright orange-red wing covers combined with its dark head and thorax create a distinctive two-toned pattern. Memory trick: 'Red wings, dark front' - like a cardinal with its red body and dark head, but in reverse.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'longhorn' can be confusing since these beetles have nothing to do with cattle - it refers purely to their extended antennae. Many people also don't realize that longhorn beetles are generally beneficial insects whose larvae help decompose dead wood in forest ecosystems.
compareHints: As the only Brachyleptura species commonly found in New England, the Red-winged Longhorn Beetle is most similar to other red longhorn beetles in different genera. However, most other red longhorns either lack the distinct two-toned coloration or have different patterns like stripes or spots rather than the solid reddish wing covers of this species.
